name: Mechanical Neck Pain
summary: Neck pain associated with movement, posture or sustained loading, without evidence that a specific serious pathology or nerve-root disorder explains the presentation.

looksLike: Pain with rotation, extension or prolonged positions
Possible referred shoulder-girdle discomfort without a consistent dermatomal pattern
redFlags: Fever, immunosuppression, cancer history or unexplained weight loss
Progressive neurological deficit, gait disturbance, hand clumsiness or bowel/bladder change
Thunderclap headache, vascular symptoms or suspected cervical artery dissection
Progressive neurological deficit or myelopathic signs
firstSteps: Explain the generally favourable course and encourage comfortable daily activity
Use relative load modification rather than immobilisation
Gentle active cervical and thoracic movement; short frequent movement breaks
selfCare: Graded return to usual activity rather than prolonged rest
Ergonomic changes only when they address a clear aggravating factor
Agree a simple written dose and progression rule the patient can follow independently

assess: Neurological screen usually normal in uncomplicated cases
Pain behavior, aggravating/relieving factors and 24-hour pattern
Cervical active ROM and repeated-movement response
Neurological screen when arm symptoms, weakness or paresthesia are present
Thoracic mobility, scapular control and relevant muscle performance
Workstation, sleep, activity and psychosocial contributors
Baseline irritability and 24-hour response to ordinary tasks; document what changes symptoms and what the patient can still do
Screen for headache, dizziness, systemic symptoms and trauma history; refer if the presentation is atypical or concerning

tests.name: Cervical Active Range of Motion
tests.purpose: Establish baseline movement, symptom response and functional restriction; it does not identify a single painful tissue.
tests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain or meaningful restriction in one or more directions.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Explain the generally favourable course and encourage comfortable daily activity
Use relative load modification rather than immobilisation
Gentle active cervical and thoracic movement; short frequent movement breaks
Address sleep, stress and work-station factors where relevant
dose: Cervical rotation/flexion in comfortable range: 5–10 reps, 3–5 times/day
Short movement breaks every 30–60 minutes as practical
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Add thoracic mobility and sensorimotor exercise when deficits are present
Graded exposure to previously provocative tasks
dose: Cervical isometrics: 5 x 5–10 seconds in 4 directions
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Build tolerance for work, driving, sport and sustained positions
Progress resistance and task duration according to response
Self-management plan for temporary symptom flares
dose: Progress resistance: 2–4 sets of 6–15 reps, 2–3 days/week
Task-specific exposure increased gradually; monitor next-day response
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Functional cervical ROM adequate for required tasks
Work, driving or sport tolerated with manageable symptoms

logic: First decide whether this is uncomplicated mechanical neck pain or whether the presentation suggests radiculopathy, myelopathy, fracture, inflammatory disease, infection or vascular pathology.
Do not choose treatment only from the pain location. Let irritability, movement loss, functional limitation and the patient's response to testing guide the plan.
Passive treatment is mainly used to create a window for active movement. Long-term recovery depends more on movement confidence, strength, endurance and load tolerance.
structures: Cervical discs, facet joints, muscles and connective tissues may contribute; symptoms are not reliably localised to one structure.
mechanism: Often multifactorial: sustained positions, sudden load changes, reduced physical capacity, sleep/stress factors or minor strain.
classification: Acute: under 6 weeks; subacute: 6–12 weeks; persistent: over 12 weeks (time categories guide communication, not tissue diagnosis).
investigations: Imaging is not routinely required for uncomplicated non-traumatic neck pain without red flags.
Arrange medical assessment and targeted imaging when serious pathology, trauma or progressive neurological deficit is suspected.
manual: Cervical/thoracic mobilization may provide short-term benefit when matched to examination findings and patient preference.
Avoid high-velocity cervical manipulation when vascular, neurological, fracture or other contraindications are present; it is not essential care.
Cervical or thoracic mobilization when indicated
Mulligan NAG/SNAG or MWM when a clear comparable sign improves
Soft-tissue techniques for short-term symptom modulation
Thrust manipulation only after appropriate advanced screening, consent and clinician training
For pain-dominant presentations, use gentle Maitland Grade I–II cervical or thoracic mobilization for 30–60 seconds × 2–4 bouts and immediately reassess.
For stiffness-dominant presentations, use a direction-specific Grade III–IV mobilization or a pain-free SNAG/MWM only when screening is clear and the patient tolerates end range.
Soft-tissue work can be used briefly over cervical/thoracic muscles when it reduces guarding; follow it immediately with active ROM.
Cervical thrust manipulation is not a text-only technique. It requires advanced practical training, informed consent and contemporary vascular/neurological risk assessment.
modalities: Heat may offer short-term comfort if preferred.
Do not rely on passive modalities or posture correction alone; active exercise and education remain central.
Heat may be used briefly for comfort in selected patients
TENS can be considered as a short-term analgesic adjunct
Avoid making passive modalities the primary treatment
Heat: commonly 10–15 minutes for comfort before movement if the patient prefers it and sensation/circulation are intact.
TENS: may be trialed for short-term analgesia using a comfortable strong sensory intensity; do not let it replace movement and exercise.
Avoid routine dependence on ultrasound or multiple passive modalities when the patient can safely participate in active care.
dosing: Cervical active ROM: 5–10 comfortable repetitions in each useful direction, 2–4 times/day in an irritable stage.
Deep neck flexor nods: 5–10-second holds × 5–10 repetitions, progressing quality before resistance.
Cervical isometrics: gentle 20–30% effort, 5–10 seconds × 5 repetitions in flexion, extension and side-bending as tolerated.
Progress toward loaded carries, pulling, pushing and task-specific endurance when symptoms remain stable.
progression: Increase range before load if highly irritable
Progress resistance and endurance when symptoms remain stable
Move from isolated control to functional lifting, work or sport tasks
Change one main training variable at a time (range, resistance, repetitions or task complexity) so the response is interpretable
Review pain, function, confidence and the 24-hour response at follow-up; progress by capacity and goals rather than a fixed session count
Progress range first when movement is highly irritable; progress load and endurance when pain is more stable.
A mild temporary increase in symptoms can be acceptable if it settles quickly and function is improving.
Advance from isolated neck/scapular exercise to work, driving, lifting or sport-specific tasks.
mistakes: Assuming posture or one palpated structure is the sole cause
Missing myelopathy or vascular warning signs
Treating every neck pain as a 'facet problem' or 'muscle spasm'.
Using too many passive techniques in one session.
Giving 8–10 home exercises that the patient will not realistically perform.
pearls: Symptoms and function matter more than a presumed isolated tissue lesion.
A normal neurological screen does not eliminate every serious cause; reassess if the pattern changes.
education: Explain that common neck pain is usually safe to move when serious pathology has been excluded.
Encourage frequent position changes instead of searching for one perfect posture.
Teach the patient what symptoms should prompt medical review, especially progressive weakness, gait change or unusual severe headache/dizziness.
escalation: Refer urgently for progressive neurological or myelopathic signs
Consider further medical assessment if severe symptoms fail to improve or the clinical picture is atypical

tests.name: Cervical Active Range of Motion
tests.purpose: Establish baseline movement, symptom response and functional restriction; it does not identify a single painful tissue.
tests.positive: Reproduction of familiar pain or meaningful restriction in one or more directions.
tests.patientPosition: Seated, supported feet, neutral starting posture; clinician observes from front and side.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Record direction, range and symptom behaviour; combine with neurological and red-flag screening.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
